hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to high-contrast, elongated linear forms or sharp geometric silhouettes presented within monochromatic, grayscale scenes. The activating features are typically distinct straight or slightly curved lines, rods, slots, or radiating appendages—such as a bright silvery rod, a pencil shaft, spider legs, or a dark pill-shaped slot—that create a stark luminosity boundary against the background. This background is consistently grainy, textured, or uniform, appearing in explicitly neutral tones of medium gray, charcoal, or deep black, while the activating features are either intensely bright white or pitch black, creating a binary contrast. The neuron is invariant to contrast polarity (activating for both light-on-dark and dark-on-light stimuli) and object identity, provided the scene preserves a graphic, noise-filled aesthetic. The linear feature typically occupies 10–50% of the image area and is most effective when traversing the frame diagonally (often from upper-left to lower-right) or horizontally across the center.
